title: An Earth-Centered Universe
objective: After this level you can describe the geocentric model and why it lasted for more than a thousand years.
summary: Ptolemy’s Earth-centered model used epicycles to match the planets and lasted about 1,400 years.

cards.headline: For 1,400 years, scholars agreed: Earth sits still at the center.
cards.body: Before you laugh, step outside. The ground feels perfectly still, and the whole sky seems to turn around you. The idea fit what people could actually see.

cards.headline: Ptolemy's universe
cards.body: Around 150 CE, Ptolemy described it in a book later known as the Almagest: Earth motionless at the center, with the Sun, Moon, planets and stars all circling it. One snag: planets sometimes seem to go backwards (Level 16's retrograde motion). Ptolemy's fix was to put each planet on a small circle, an epicycle, that itself moved around Earth. Think of a teacup ride: you spin on a platform that is also spinning.

cards.headline: Why it made sense
cards.body: First, you can't feel Earth moving. Second, there was a sharp test. If Earth orbited the Sun, nearby stars should shift slightly over a year, the way a nearby tree shifts against distant hills as you walk past. Nobody could detect that shift, called parallax. No shift, so no motion, it seemed. And the model predicted planet positions well enough to run calendars for centuries. Wrong, but very useful.

mascot.line: Remember this missing shift. In Level 30, someone finally sees it.

cards.headline: Geocentric model: understood
learned: Ptolemy put a motionless Earth at the center
No one could feel Earth move or see stellar parallax

questions.prompt: In Ptolemy’s model, what sat at the center of the universe?

options.label: The Moon
options.rationale: The Moon circled Earth in his model.

options.label: The Milky Way
options.rationale: Ptolemy didn’t know our galaxy’s structure.

questions.explanation: Ptolemy’s geocentric model put a motionless Earth at the center, with everything else circling it.

questions.prompt: Why did the lack of an observed stellar shift (parallax) seem to support an Earth-centered universe?

options.label: Stars were thought to be too dim to measure precisely
options.rationale: Stars were plainly visible; the issue was their positions.

options.label: Parallax was thought to happen only near the equator
options.rationale: Parallax would show from anywhere on a moving Earth.

options.label: A moving Earth should shift nearby stars, and none moved
Epicycles were thought to cancel out any parallax
options.rationale: Epicycles were for planets, not star shifts.

questions.explanation: If Earth orbited the Sun, nearby stars should appear to shift during the year. Nobody could detect that, so a still Earth seemed more reasonable.

questions.prompt: From Level 16: how did Ptolemy’s model explain retrograde motion?

options.label: Earth overtaking the outer planets
options.rationale: That’s the modern explanation; Ptolemy’s Earth didn’t move.

options.label: Planets truly reversing direction for a while
options.rationale: Planets in his model circled continuously.

options.label: The Moon passing in front of the planets
options.rationale: The Moon played no part in it.

options.label: Planets riding epicycles as they circled Earth

questions.explanation: With Earth fixed, Ptolemy had each planet loop on a small epicycle, producing apparent backwards motion. Today we know it’s Earth overtaking them.
